subject: mathematics
question_text: If sec θ + tan θ = 2/3, find sin θ and state the quadrant in which θ lies.

mark_split.label: Get sec θ − tan θ from the identity
Find sin θ and fix the quadrant

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 12, book p.84. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split rewards the reciprocal pair sec θ − tan θ = 3/2 first and the value of sin θ together with the quadrant second, because the question asks for two things and the quadrant is not a free extra. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1 to Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, under the 2026-27 pattern; Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Checked numerically: sec θ = 13/12 and tan θ = −5/12 give sec θ + tan θ = 0.6666666667 = 2/3 and sec θ − tan θ = 1.5000000000 = 3/2; sin θ = −5/13 = −0.3846153846 and cos θ = 12/13 = 0.9230769231 satisfy sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. The angle is θ = −22.6198649480°, that is 337.3801350520°, which is in the fourth quadrant, so the quadrant on the page is derived from the two signs and not asserted.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name the identity you use, and say how you decide the quadrant.

steps.label: Get sec θ − tan θ from the identity
steps.margin_note: First mark. sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 factors into the given expression times its partner, so the partner is the reciprocal 3/2. The given value 2/3 is not 0, so the division is allowed.
steps.memory_tip: sec θ + tan θ and sec θ − tan θ multiply to 1, so each is the reciprocal of the other. Given 2/3, the partner is 3/2.
lines: sec θ and tan θ appear, so cos θ ≠ 0.

recall.must_convey: That sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 makes sec θ − tan θ the reciprocal of the given 2/3, so it is 3/2.
accept: sec squared minus tan squared is one so the two brackets are reciprocals and the other one is three by two
use sec squared theta minus tan squared theta equals one and factorise
the partner of two by three is three by two

steps.why: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 says the two expressions sec θ + tan θ and sec θ − tan θ have product 1, so each is the reciprocal of the other. One given value therefore fixes both, and two linear equations follow.
common_mistakes: Writing sec θ − tan θ = −3/2 by taking the wrong sign.
Using sec²θ + tan²θ = 1, which is not an identity.

steps.label: Find sin θ and fix the quadrant
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Adding gives sec θ = 13/12, subtracting gives tan θ = −5/12, and sin θ = tan θ cos θ = −5/13. cos θ positive with sin θ negative happens only in the fourth quadrant.
steps.memory_tip: Add the two equations to get sec θ, subtract them to get tan θ. Then sin θ = tan θ × cos θ, and the two signs name the quadrant.
lines: cos θ is positive and sin θ is negative,
and that happens only in the fourth quadrant.

lines.text: ∴ sin θ = −5/13, θ in the fourth quadrant

recall.must_convey: That sin θ = −5/13, and that cos θ positive with sin θ negative places θ in the fourth quadrant.
accept: add to get sec theta twelve by thirteen for cos and subtract to get tan minus five by twelve so sin is minus five by thirteen
sin theta is minus five over thirteen and theta is in the fourth quadrant
cos is positive and sin is negative so it is the fourth quadrant
add cheste sec theta, subtract cheste tan theta, sin theta minus five by thirteen
sin theta equals minus five by thirteen, fourth quadrant

steps.why: The two linear equations give sec θ and tan θ, and sin θ = tan θ × cos θ. The quadrant is then read off the two signs: cos θ positive together with sin θ negative occurs in the fourth quadrant and nowhere else.
common_mistakes: Answering sin θ = 5/13 and losing the minus sign.
Naming the second quadrant, where cos θ is negative.
Stating a quadrant without checking the signs of both sin θ and cos θ.
